commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. content.content:
# Container Environment

## Pitch

A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it tries.

## Description

Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and questions from the Ask tab always run in a container, and are the only runs that do. Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code step always run on the host, as the [HarnessIntegration](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, with their protected locations, and never need Podman. Freeform tasks always run on the host, and so do the application's own runs, the one-off runs, the palette's file search, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles, which change nothing.
Whatever runs in a container, the application itself still works on the host: it builds the spec before a task, takes the task's snapshots and lists the files it changed, shows diffs, and makes commits there, as ever.

## Runtime

The container runtime is Podman or Docker, whichever is in use: run through the `podman` or the `docker` command, and no other. Each run is one `run --rm` of the harness's command by that runtime, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over. Wherever this spec names Podman, a `podman` command, or a Podman machine, it means the runtime in use, Docker's own equivalent standing in for it while Docker is, as below; everything else is the same whichever runs the containers.

## Choosing Runtime

Which runtime is in use is picked in the Containers section of the [SettingsWindow](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window): "Automatic", "Podman", or "Docker", Automatic until another is picked, remembered for the user, as the [UserPreferences](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences) says, not for a project. Automatic is worked out at each launch, and again whenever the settings or the welcome checks look: the first of Podman and Docker that is installed and can run a container for the user, Podman first where both can, since it runs rootless on Linux. Where neither can, nothing is picked, and what needs a container fails saying neither is available, with links to install either, as a missing Podman does below. Podman or Docker picked by hand is used whether or not it is working, and its runs fail saying why where it isn't. A run already going when the runtime changes finishes with the one it started with; the next run uses the new one, building its image there first where it has none.

## User And Files

On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`; Docker runs the container as the user, with `--user` given the user's id and group, and the harness's home a directory owned by that id. Either way every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine and Docker in Docker Desktop's virtual machine, each a virtual machine the runtime

### Manages

where Docker Desktop isn't running, the run says so and

offers "Start Docker", which starts it, as "Start Podman" does for a Podman machine. There too, what a run writes to the project belongs to the user, as the [Application](../application/index.md#application) says of every file the application

### Creates

the container runs as the user rather than as root inside

the machine, and a file it writes into a folder mounted from Windows is the user's, owned by them and inheriting the folder's permissions, never owned by Administrators or another account. Where this spec mounts a volume so the user owns it, with Podman's `:U`, Docker gives it to the user's id when the application creates it, by a short `chown` run in a throwaway container before the volume is first used.

## Resources

Every container, image, and volume the application makes, with whichever runtime, is labelled `io.suspense.app=suspense`, and its name begins with `suspense-`, so the application can always find what is its own and never touches what isn't. Images are tagged `suspense-default` and, for a project with a Containerfile of its own, `suspense-project-` and a short hash of the project's path; volumes are named `suspense-` and the harness, as `suspense-claude`. Runs are always `--rm`, so a container is left only while it runs, or where a run was cut off, as by a crash.

## Missing Podman

Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegration](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.

## Podman Machine

On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

## Podman Access

Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed. The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written, what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead. The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that the build failed.

## Image

Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run `piton build` to check its work.
A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what its runs in a container need, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.
The image is a Linux image, whatever the host is, so what it holds is installed in it for Linux, for the architecture Podman runs: each harness and piton at the version found on the host, from its own Linux release or package, never a binary copied from the host, which on macOS or Windows can't run in it. The build is given only the Containerfile the application writes for it, in a build context of its own, a fresh temporary directory holding nothing else, never the project or the user's home, and needs nothing from the host but the network.
Each harness is installed in a step of its own, so one that can't be installed never stops the others. A version taken from the host is used only once the package registry is asked, before the build, and has it, as `npm view <package>@<version> version` answering it; the version a host's command prints is read only as a plain version number, never with anything printed around it. ## Pitch

A container the application owns, that a run of the harness works in, so each mode sees only what it may use. What a run can read or change comes from what is mounted into its container, never from its prompt, a deny rule, or a guard: a container with no code in it can't read the code or change it, whatever the harness is and whatever it tries.

## Description

Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and questions from the Ask tab always run in a container, and are the only runs that do. The container runtime is Podman or Docker, whichever is in use: run through the `podman` or the `docker` command, and no other. Each run is one `run --rm` of the harness's command by that runtime, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over. What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing else from the host. So a harness that keys its sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What each kind of run is given, as the [ProjectLocations](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations) names the locations, follows.

### Spec

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write, for the same reason, bound in from the project itself, never an empty, temporary, or copied one, so the manifest a build in the container starts from is the host's, and what it writes there is the host's next build's, the application creating the directory in the project first where it isn't there; the Suspense fluency file, read only; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it places the shape's guidance in.
Unless the project lets its Spec runs read the code, a setting of the project's, off until switched on in the [SettingsWindow](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window)'s Containers section and saved with the project's data. While it is on, a Spec run is given the code location too, read only, as a question is, mounted in its place, so the harness can read the code the spec describes but never change it, and the scratch directory, writable, is mounted over the code location's guidance files alone, its CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md files, so `piton build` writes its shape guidance there rather than into the code. Where the code location holds the spec location, as `./`, the spec location is still mounted read and write over it, and the project's data still left out. Every other mount is as above, and what the run may write is unchanged: only the spec, the reference, `.piton`, and its understanding file. The setting takes effect from the next run; a run already going keeps the mounts it started with.
A second setting of the project's, also off until switched on, and offered only while the first is on, lets its Spec runs read the whole project as well: the project directory is then mounted at `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, read only, beneath every other mount, so everything in it, its README, its build files, its scripts, its documentation, and whatever lies outside the code and spec locations, can be read, and nothing of it changed. A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container, and the Suspense fluency file, read only. Where one of the code location and the spec location holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither is hidden from the question by the other.

Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.
Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both the code location and the spec location.

On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path, `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl` standing for the project directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. Only a path that is `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, or begins with `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/`, is mapped, never text that merely holds it, as `/workspace-old`. ## Logging In

When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. The login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser, once, and nothing else ever opens one.
Only the login command's own output is read for it, from when the command starts, never what the image build prints before it, nor anything Podman prints while it pulls, builds, or starts the container, all of which is shown as text and never opened, its URLs at most clickable links. And only a URL that is the harness's login is opened: the first one the login command prints that leads to its sign-in, as Claude Code's to claude.ai or console.anthropic.com, Codex's to auth.openai.com, or OpenCode's to the provider it is logging in with, or a localhost callback it asks to be visited. Any other URL it prints, as a link to documentation, release notes, or a package's homepage, is only shown. A login opens at most one URL by itself, the first such one; any later is shown as a link, for the user to click. Where no URL is recognized, nothing opens, and the view shows every URL the command printed as a link instead.
Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
A login needs the image, as any run in a container does, and the first login on a machine is most often the first thing to need it. So the login view builds it first where it isn't there or is out of date, showing "Preparing environment" and what the build prints as it goes, and starts the login command only once the build has succeeded. A build that fails shows why in the login view, as a failed build says it, with a "Try again" button that builds it again, and starts no login.
The harness's volume is ready for it before its first login: created by the application with `podman volume create` where it isn't there, and mounted so that the user the container runs as owns it and can write it, as with Podman's `:U` option, never left owned by root where the harness runs as the user. The container's HOME, where the volume is mounted beneath it, as ~/.claude, is a directory that user owns, as is the volume, so the login command can write its credentials there on the first login as on any other.
Which harness is logged in is always the one the run needs: the harness of the run's project, as the [HarnessIntegration](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, never Claude Code by default, and never another project's. A run, a Welcome check, or a login asked for checks that harness's own volume alone, by its own credentials file: Claude Code's `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, Codex's `~/.codex/auth.json`, and OpenCode's `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`, each counting as logged in only where the file is there and not empty. Its login view is titled for it, "Log in to Codex" and the like, and runs its own login command, `claude /login` for Claude Code, `codex login` for Codex, and `opencode auth login` for OpenCode, in a container with that harness's volume mounted, so its credentials land where its runs read them. A run never asks for one harness's login while it is about to run another.
A run that fails because its harness isn't logged in says so, naming the harness, "Codex isn't logged in", with a "Log in" button that shows its login view, rather than the harness's raw error alone. A login that fails says why in the command's own words, its exit status, and which harness it was for, and the run waiting on it fails saying the same. The login view, the Welcome check, and the Settings rows all read the same volume for a harness, so a harness that is logged in shows as logged in everywhere, and one that isn't never shows as logged in anywhere.
The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindow](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.

## Guards

A run in a container has no protected locations, as the [HarnessIntegration](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) names them: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location, since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, name only what it can see. Runs on the host keep their protected locations as ever.

## Spec Build

A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work in the refreshed reference, and that build succeeds whenever the spec is sound: it owns the reference files it finds, through the manifest in the mounted `.piton` directory, and places the shape's guidance in the scratch directory standing in for the code location, where it goes nowhere. A build there that fails fails only because of the spec, never because of what the container leaves out, so its errors are the run's own to fix. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over, however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as the [SpecBuild](../spec-build/index.md#spec-build) says, so the host's reference and shape guidance are those of the spec as the run left it.

Every container we create today is a short-lived `run --rm` (removed when it exits), labelled `io.suspense.app=suspense` and named `suspense-…`. None are kept running, and none are reused between runs. Five things create one:

1. **One per Spec or Ask run.** A Spec task, a Chain prompt's spec step or follow-up, and an Ask question each get their own container (`run_args` at `src/container.rs:447`, called from `src/harness.rs:1323`). Code tasks, Freeform tasks and the app's own small runs stay on the host and never create one. The spec requires one container per run, because each run's mounts are what it's allowed to see.
2. **Login checks: one tiny container per check.** `container::logged_in` (`src/container.rs:2285`) starts a container just to run `test -s` on the credentials file. Before each run, `harness.rs:1620` caches a positive answer, so it fires only until the harness is logged in. The Welcome page (`welcome.rs:234`) and the Settings rows (`settings_window.rs:491`) don't cache it, so they create one container per harness every time they check.
3. **After each image build: one container per bundled command.** `check_commands` (`src/container.rs:2134`) runs `--version` for claude, codex, opencode and piton in a separate container each, so four per build. This only happens when an image is rebuilt.
4. **Docker only: one `chown` container per new volume.** This runs once, when the volume is first created (`src/container.rs:2254`), and is skipped if the volume already exists. Podman doesn't need it because it uses `:U`.
5. **Logging in: one container per login.**

Checking whether Podman or Docker is available uses `podman info` / `docker info` and doesn't create a container.

The avoidable waste is mostly in items 2 and 3. The Welcome and Settings login checks could share the cache that runs already use, or read the volume without starting a container. The four version checks could run in a single container.
